tagline.text: Sunrise over a sea of clouds and the Milky Way from Luzon's highest peak

location.label: Location
location.text: Kabayan–Bokod, Benguet (bordering Ifugao and Nueva Vizcaya)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–March (dry season, high chance of a sea of clouds)

items.credit: Say Bernardo / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: At about

, this is Luzon's highest peak and the third-highest mountain in the Philippines. It's famous for the sea of clouds spreading beneath the summit at dawn, the sunrise, and the sky full of stars, and it's a national park that requires advance booking and a medical certificate.
Mount Pulag is the highest peak of the central Cordillera range, where the borders of Benguet, Ifugao, and Nueva Vizcaya provinces meet. At about
, it is the highest point on the island of Luzon and the third-highest mountain in the Philippines after Mount Apo and Mount Dulang-dulang in Mindanao. It was designated a national park in
, and the Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) strictly manages the number of climbers and the rules.

What makes this mountain special is the "sea of clouds" you meet at the summit at dawn. On days with low temperatures and just the right humidity, the valleys below the mountain fill with clouds, and the moment the sun rises, it feels as if you're standing above a white ocean. Instead of trees, the summit is covered in an endless expanse of low "dwarf bamboo" grassland, giving it an atmosphere hard to believe belongs to a tropical Southeast Asian mountain, and on clear nights the Milky Way is vividly visible.

For the local Ibaloi and Kalanguya indigenous peoples, Pulag is a sacred mountain where the spirits of their ancestors reside. Shouting or leaving trash at the summit is considered an insult to indigenous culture, and this is the very first point emphasized in the national park orientation.

The gentlest trail, the Ambangeg trail, can be attempted with reasonable fitness even without much climbing experience, making it a popular choice as a "first high-altitude climb." The Akiki and Tawangan trails, on the other hand, are for experienced climbers. If you just bring gear to withstand near-freezing cold, you'll be rewarded with one of the most impressive dawns in the Philippines.

blocks.title: Summit sunrise and sea of clouds

children.text: Setting off around
2 AM
and reaching the summit by around
, you'll see the eastern sky turn red as the sun rises above the sea of clouds. Depending on the weather, there may be no sea of clouds at all, so it's best to keep your expectations in check.
From above Camp 2 all the way to the summit, knee-high bamboo grassland stretches along a gentle ridge. Many people find the golden grassland seen while descending after sunrise even more beautiful.

blocks.title: Passing through moss forest and pine forest

children.text: The stretch climbing from the ranger station to camp alternates between Benguet pine forest and mist-soaked moss forest. Trees covered in ferns, orchids, and moss create a scene like something out of a fairy tale.

With almost no light pollution at this altitude, the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye on clear dry-season nights. Bring a tripod and you can capture star photos around the camp or ranger station.
A mandatory session before climbing, covering Pulag's ecology, indigenous culture, and safety rules. It's not just a formality but a good chance to understand the mountain, so listen closely.

blocks.title: Taking on the Akiki trail (experienced climbers)

children.text: The Akiki trail, which starts from Kabayan, is nicknamed the "killer trail" for its steep grades and long distance. Over
3 days, 2 nights
, you cross rivers and pass through old-growth forest before reaching the summit, which brings a great sense of achievement.

blocks.title: Combining with the Kabayan Mummy Caves

children.text: The fire-cured mummies of Kabayan (a traditional Ibaloi burial heritage), which you can visit before or after the climb, add extra depth to a Pulag trip.

From Manila to Baguio by bus takes about
4–6 hours
(fare around
). From Baguio to the DENR Visitor Center in Bokod, a chartered van or jeepney takes about
2–3 hours
; a charter costs around
round trip per vehicle, so it's usually split among your group.

There is public transport toward Kabayan and Bokod near the Slaughter Compound bus terminal in Baguio, but it's hard to time it for the orientation and you'd need separate transport to the ranger station, so it isn't recommended.
The most practical option is a join tour departing from Manila or Baguio. Packages that include DENR reservation handling, a guide, transport, and homestay run about
per person, and are run every weekend by numerous hiking clubs and travel agencies.

items.title: From the visitor center to the ranger station

children.text: After the orientation, it's about
25–40 minutes
to Babadak Ranger Station (at about
above sea level) along an unpaved mountain road, traveled by habal-habal or 4x4. A habal-habal ride costs around
per person.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK); from there it's about
3–4 hours
by bus to Baguio, and then a further
2–3 hours
to the visitor center.
The best chance of seeing a sea of clouds is during the dry season,
December–March
. At this time, dawn temperatures at the summit are around
, and in January and
February

they can drop below freezing, sometimes leaving frost on the grassland. Because this is the most popular time, weekend slots book out months in advance, and competition is especially fierce around New Year and Holy Week.
April–May

has mild weather and many clear days, making it comfortable for climbing, though the frequency of the sea of clouds drops a little, and dry conditions can lead to access being restricted due to wildfire risk. During the rainy season,
June–October

, typhoons and heavy rain close the mountain on many days, and even when it's open, poor visibility often blocks the summit view. The national park also sometimes schedules rest periods for ecological recovery, so be sure to check the latest notices on PAMO's official page before setting out.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Climbing Pulag usually means sleeping at a homestay near the ranger station and heading to the summit before dawn. Homestays are simple lodges with shared bunks and blankets provided, costing about

per person, and hot showers are hard to come by. Tent camping at Camp 1 and Camp 2 has allowed days and numbers that change from season to season, so check when you book. Spending a night in Baguio before the climb to acclimatize to the altitude is also a good idea.

There are no restaurants on the mountain, so you either eat what the homestay provides (rice, sauteed vegetables, chicken adobo, and the like) or bring your own food. Before the pre-dawn climb, a warm soup, oatmeal, or a cup of Benguet coffee makes a big difference. Buy plenty of high-calorie snacks such as chocolate, nuts, and energy bars at the market in Baguio or Bokod.
Make your DENR reservation at least a few weeks before your climb date, and months ahead for peak-season weekends. If booking on your own is difficult, use a certified join tour.
The medical certificate ("fit to climb") must be issued shortly before your climb date; without one, you'll be denied entry regardless of your reservation.

Prepare cold-weather gear in layers. Thermal base layers, a fleece, a windproof/waterproof jacket, gloves, a beanie, and thick socks are the basics. Avoid cotton clothing, since it draws away body heat once soaked with sweat.
A headlamp and spare batteries are essential. Walking the pre-dawn trail without light is simply not possible.
There is almost no phone signal on the mountain. Bring plenty of portable battery packs, and let your family know your schedule in advance.
Staying at the summit too long quickly drops your body temperature. Bringing a thermos of hot water helps a great deal.
Drone flights are banned without a national park permit, so check with PAMO in advance.
The summit of Pulag can drop below freezing at dawn. Hypothermia is actually the most common danger, so if you lack proper cold-weather gear, it's wise to postpone the climb.
If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or asthma, be sure to consult a doctor. Climbing to nearly
can bring on mild altitude symptoms.
Don't stray off the designated trail or trample and damage the dwarf bamboo grassland. All trash must be carried back out.
Campfires and cooking fires are banned except where designated, and rules are even stricter during the dry season because of wildfire risk.
If a typhoon or heavy rain is forecast, the climb can be canceled without notice. Check the non-refundable terms before you book.
Because this is an indigenous sacred site, refrain from loud noise, drinking, and reckless drone flying at the summit.
About
2–3 hours
by car from the visitor center, a highland city good for resting and acclimatizing before or after the climb.
Near Kabayan town, a cultural heritage site where you can see centuries-old fire-cured Ibaloi mummies.
South of Baguio, a good day-trek ridge route for warming up before Pulag.
About
5–6 hours
from Baguio by bus, a mountain village with caves, hanging coffins, and sunrise spots.
